title: Sources, Safe Centres, Custom Ellipses, Swipes & Scopes
description: The element that started a navigation, alignment that won't strand content, a writable ellipsis, swipe-revealed actions, and per-tree registries.

drops.title: The Link That Starts It
drops.description: Chrome 156's :navigation-source keeps the clicked element matched for the whole navigation, so it can name itself the hero.
drops.concept: Shared-element page transitions normally need the clicked item's identity carried across a navigation by hand — a data attribute, sessionStorage, a router hook. :navigation-source makes the browser hold it for you: the link, button or form that began the navigation stays matched for its duration, so one CSS rule gives it the view-transition-name. Six tiles morph into a detail view here, with duration, easing and hero naming all tunable, and the pseudo-class mirrored in JS where it hasn't shipped.
drops.source: Web Standards — What's new in Chrome 156

interaction.mouse: Hover the tiles; the panel retimes the transition live
interaction.click: Click any tile to transition into it, then Back or Replay
interaction.touch: Tap a tile — same transition, same source highlight

drops.title: Centred Until It Overflows
drops.description: Plain center strands half the overflow past the scroll origin; safe center gives up and aligns to start instead.
drops.concept: A centred flex row that outgrows its container overflows both ways, and the left half sits before the scroll origin where no scrollbar can follow. The safe keyword makes the alignment fall back to start exactly when that would happen, and unsafe is the explicit opt-in to clipping — Safari 27.2 has just extended both to pair with normal. Three rails, a width slider and a live readout of how many pixels of the first chip are unreachable.

interaction.mouse: Drag the rail width, chip count and gap and watch the clipped readout
interaction.click: Scroll each rail to prove which content can actually be reached
interaction.touch: Swipe the rails horizontally; the panel stacks under the demo

drops.title: The Ellipsis, In Your Own Words
drops.description: Chrome 157 lets text-overflow take a string, so a clipped line can end in “ (more)”, an arrow or anything you type.
drops.concept: For twenty years the only thing a browser could say at the edge of a box was “…”. The string value of text-overflow replaces the measure-and-slice JavaScript every card component ends up writing, and it keeps the truncation inside the line box where it belongs. Five rows show different markers, including one you type, with a hidden-probe fallback producing the identical output where the value hasn't shipped.
drops.source: Chrome 157 release notes — text-overflow string value

interaction.mouse: Slide the box width and font-size to force truncation at different points
interaction.click: Type your own marker string into the panel
interaction.touch: All controls stack below the demo on narrow screens

drops.title: Swipe, And The Menu Is There
drops.description: Open UI's overscroll-actions proposal turns the iOS row-swipe into markup — with the panel inert until it opens.
drops.concept: Swipe-to-reveal is everywhere on phones and nowhere in HTML, so every list rebuilds it from pointer events. The Declarative Overscroll Actions explainer proposes overscrollcontainer and overscrollarea attributes, a command="toggle-overscroll" invoker, a ::overscroll-backdrop that dismisses, and modality so closed panels stay out of the tab order. This rebuilds the behaviour on scroll snapping today, logging the lifecycle events the proposal defines.
drops.source: Open UI — Declarative Overscroll Actions explainer

interaction.mouse: Drag a row to the left, or press its ⋯ invoker
interaction.click: Tap the row body — the backdrop puts it back; actions close it too
interaction.touch: Swipe a row exactly as you would in a mail app

drops.title: One Tag Name, Four Components
drops.description: Scoped custom element registries landed in Firefox 159 today, so <ui-chip> can mean something different in every shadow tree.
drops.concept: One global registry means one definition of a tag name for the whole page, and the second define() of that name throws. A CustomElementRegistry per shadow tree ends the fight: the same <ui-chip> markup renders as pills, switches, meters or stamps depending on which tree it was parsed into. The demo also triggers the global collision on purpose so you can read the error it replaces.
drops.source: Chrome for Developers — Make custom elements behave with scoped registries

interaction.mouse: Hover the scopes to compare four readings of the same markup
interaction.click: Add a chip to every scope, force the global collision, rebuild the trees
interaction.touch: Scopes stack into one column; all buttons are tap targets
